### equate.evaluate.benchmark.load_benchmark(name, \*\*config)

Build a registered benchmark (`config` goes to its loader).

* **Return type:**
  [`Benchmark`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.benchmark.html.md#equate.evaluate.benchmark.Benchmark)


# _autosummary/equate.evaluate.html.md

# equate.evaluate

Evaluate matchers honestly: metrics, leakage-aware splits, and a benchmark harness.

Dependency-light (numpy/scipy only; sklearn is used for ARI / V-measure when present).
Precision and recall always travel together ([`Scores`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.html.md#equate.evaluate.Scores)), the pairwise and cluster
granularities are explicit ([`pairs_to_labels()`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.html.md#equate.evaluate.pairs_to_labels) converts on purpose), B³ is the
default cluster metric, thresholds are selected on validation data by a separate call,
and [`benchmark_matcher()`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.html.md#equate.evaluate.benchmark_matcher) splits by entity so test entities are unseen.
See `docs/research/14-evaluation-benchmarks-and-methodology.md`.

```pycon
>>> from equate.evaluate import pairwise_prf, bcubed
>>> pairwise_prf([(0, 0), (1, 1)], [(0, 0), (1, 2)]).f1
0.5
```

### Functions

| [`pairwise_prf`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.html.md#equate.evaluate.pairwise_prf)(pred_pairs, true_pairs, \*[, ...])    | Pairwise precision / recall / F1 of predicted pairs against gold pairs.          |
|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`bcubed`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.html.md#equate.evaluate.bcubed)(pred_labels, true_labels)                   | B³ precision / recall / F1 — the default cluster metric.                         |
| [`ceaf`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.html.md#equate.evaluate.ceaf)(pred_labels, true_labels, \*[, variant, ...]) | CEAF: score the best one-to-one alignment of predicted to true clusters.         |
| [`cluster_metrics`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.html.md#equate.evaluate.cluster_metrics)(pred_labels, true_labels, \*)      | B³ (the headline), CEAF-e, ARI, V-measure, homogeneity and completeness.         |
| [`blocking_metrics`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.html.md#equate.evaluate.blocking_metrics)(candidate_pairs, ...[, n_b])      | Return `{pair_completeness, reduction_ratio, pairs_quality, n_candidates}`.      |
| [`pr_auc`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.html.md#equate.evaluate.pr_auc)(scores, y_true)                             | Average precision: the area under the precision-recall step curve.               |
| [`select_threshold`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.html.md#equate.evaluate.select_threshold)(scores, y_true, \*[, optimize])   | The score threshold (`score >= t` predicts a match) that maximises `optimize`.   |
| [`ranking_metrics`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.html.md#equate.evaluate.ranking_metrics)(ranked, gold, \*[, ks])            | Recall@k, MRR and MAP for ranked candidate lists.                                |
| [`pairs_to_labels`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.html.md#equate.evaluate.pairs_to_labels)(pairs, \*, n)                      | Cluster label per record `0..n-1` from the transitive closure of `pairs`.        |
| [`labels_to_pairs`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.html.md#equate.evaluate.labels_to_pairs)(labels)                            | Every within-cluster pair `(i, j)` with `i < j`.                                 |
| [`cross_pairs_to_labels`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.html.md#equate.evaluate.cross_pairs_to_labels)(pairs, \*, n_a, n_b)         | Labels over `A + B` (B's records offset by `n_a`) from two-table `(i, j)` pairs. |
| [`entity_split`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.html.md#equate.evaluate.entity_split)(entity_ids, \*[, ratios, seed])       | Split records into train / val / test by entity, never by record or pair.        |

### equate.evaluate.bcubed(pred_labels, true_labels)

B³ precision / recall / F1 — the default cluster metric.

Per record: precision is the share of its predicted cluster that truly belongs with
it, recall the share of its true cluster that the prediction kept with it; both are
averaged over records.

* **Return type:**
  [`Scores`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.scores.html.md#equate.evaluate.scores.Scores)

```pycon
>>> s = bcubed([0, 0, 1, 1], [0, 0, 0, 1])
>>> round(s.precision, 3), round(s.recall, 3)
(0.75, 0.667)
```

### equate.evaluate.benchmark_matcher(matcher=None, , on=('toy_names',), n_seeds=3, ratios=(0.6, 0.2, 0.2), fit=None)

Score `matcher` on unseen-entity test splits of each benchmark in `on`.

`matcher(a, b)` returns `(i, j)` pairs (a [`Matching`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.Matching)
qualifies); the default is `equate.match()`. `on` is a benchmark name, a
[`Benchmark`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.html.md#equate.evaluate.Benchmark), or an iterable of either. Scores are pairwise; a seed whose test
part has no gold pair is skipped with a warning, and a benchmark with no scorable
seed is an error. For each of `n_seeds` seeds the records of `a + b`
are split by entity (`ratios` = train/val/test); only the **test** part is
matched and scored, so a test entity was never seen in training.

`fit(train_a, train_b, train_pairs, val_a, val_b, val_pairs) -> matcher` makes the
harness train per seed: it gets the train and validation parts only (the split is
asserted leak-free first), and the matcher it returns is scored on test. Choose a
threshold on the validation part there ([`select_threshold()`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.html.md#equate.evaluate.select_threshold)),
never on test.

* **Return type:**
  [`BenchmarkReport`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.benchmark.html.md#equate.evaluate.benchmark.BenchmarkReport)

```pycon
>>> report = benchmark_matcher(n_seeds=2)
>>> s = report.summary()['toy_names']
>>> s['f1'][0] > 0.8, s['n_seeds']
(True, 2)
```

### equate.evaluate.blocking_metrics(candidate_pairs, true_pairs, , n_a, n_b=None)

Return `{pair_completeness, reduction_ratio, pairs_quality, n_candidates}`.

- **pair_completeness (PC)** = `|candidates ∩ true| / |true|` — blocking *recall*
  (upper-bounds end-to-end recall);
- **reduction_ratio (RR)** = `1 - |candidates| / |all pairs|` — how much blocking pruned;
- **pairs_quality (PQ)** = `|candidates ∩ true| / |candidates|` — blocking *precision*.

`n_b=None` means a self-join (dedup) over `n_a` items, so
`|all pairs| = n_a*(n_a-1)/2`; otherwise `|all pairs| = n_a*n_b`. For a self-join,
pairs are canonicalized to unordered `(min, max)` so orientation doesn’t matter and
`(i, j)` / `(j, i)` count once. Empty `true_pairs` yields `pair_completeness=1.0`
(vacuously perfect recall); `reduction_ratio` is clamped to `[0, 1]`.

```pycon
>>> m = blocking_metrics([(0, 0), (1, 1)], [(0, 0), (1, 1), (2, 2)], n_a=3, n_b=3)
>>> round(m['pair_completeness'], 2), round(m['pairs_quality'], 2)
(0.67, 1.0)
```

### equate.evaluate.ceaf(pred_labels, true_labels, , variant='entity', matcher='optimal')

CEAF: score the best one-to-one alignment of predicted to true clusters.

`variant='entity'` (CEAF-e, φ4) weighs each aligned pair by
`2|K∩R| / (|K|+|R|)` and normalises by the number of clusters;
`variant='mention'` (CEAF-m, φ3) weighs by `|K∩R|` and normalises by the
number of records. The alignment is a maximum-weight assignment, resolved through
equate’s [`matchers`](_autosummary/equate.matching.html.md#equate.matching.matchers) registry (`matcher`), never a
private Hungarian.

* **Return type:**
  [`Scores`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.scores.html.md#equate.evaluate.scores.Scores)

```pycon
>>> round(ceaf([0, 0, 1, 1], [0, 0, 0, 1]).f1, 3)
0.733
```

### equate.evaluate.cluster_metrics(pred_labels, true_labels, , backend='auto')

B³ (the headline), CEAF-e, ARI, V-measure, homogeneity and completeness.

`backend='auto'` uses `sklearn.metrics` for ARI / V-measure when sklearn is
installed and the numpy implementations otherwise; `'numpy'` forces the latter,
`'sklearn'` requires the former. The two agree; the choice only exists so the
core install needs neither.

* **Return type:**
  [`dict`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#dict)

```pycon
>>> m = cluster_metrics([0, 0, 1, 1], [0, 0, 0, 1], backend='numpy')
>>> sorted(m)
['ari', 'b3_f1', 'b3_precision', 'b3_recall', 'ceaf_e_f1', 'completeness',
 'homogeneity', 'v_measure']
```

### equate.evaluate.cross_pairs_to_labels(pairs, , n_a, n_b)

Labels over `A + B` (B’s records offset by `n_a`) from two-table `(i, j)` pairs.

The bridge from a matching between two collections to the entity view a cluster
metric or an entity split needs.

* **Return type:**
  [`list`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#list)[[`int`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)]

```pycon
>>> cross_pairs_to_labels([(0, 1)], n_a=2, n_b=2)
[0, 1, 2, 0]
```

### equate.evaluate.entity_split(entity_ids, , ratios=(0.6, 0.2, 0.2), seed=0)

Split records into train / val / test by entity, never by record or pair.

`entity_ids[i]` is record `i`’s true entity (e.g. from
[`cross_pairs_to_labels()`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.html.md#equate.evaluate.cross_pairs_to_labels) over a two-table gold matching).
Entities, not records, are shuffled (`seed`) and cut by `ratios`, so the parts
are disjoint in entities and roughly — not exactly — proportional in records.

* **Return type:**
  [`Split`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.split.html.md#equate.evaluate.split.Split)

```pycon
>>> s = entity_split([0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 6], seed=1)
>>> assert_no_leakage([0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 6], s.train, s.test)
>>> sorted(s.train + s.val + s.test) == list(range(10))
True
```

### equate.evaluate.labels_to_pairs(labels)

Every within-cluster pair `(i, j)` with `i < j`.

* **Return type:**
  [`set`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#set)[[`tuple`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#tuple)[[`int`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int), [`int`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)]]

```pycon
>>> sorted(labels_to_pairs([0, 0, 1, 0]))
[(0, 1), (0, 3), (1, 3)]
```

### equate.evaluate.list_benchmarks()

Names of the registered benchmarks.

* **Return type:**
  [`list`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#list)[[`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)]

### equate.evaluate.load_benchmark(name, \*\*config)

Build a registered benchmark (`config` goes to its loader).

* **Return type:**
  [`Benchmark`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.benchmark.html.md#equate.evaluate.benchmark.Benchmark)

### equate.evaluate.pairs_to_labels(pairs, , n)

Cluster label per record `0..n-1` from the transitive closure of `pairs`.

Labels are canonical: numbered in order of each cluster’s smallest record, so two
pair sets that induce the same partition give equal label lists. A record no pair
mentions is a singleton.

* **Return type:**
  [`list`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#list)[[`int`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)]

```pycon
>>> pairs_to_labels([(0, 1), (1, 2), (4, 5)], n=6)
[0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 2]
```

### equate.evaluate.pairwise_prf(pred_pairs, true_pairs, , self_join=False)

Pairwise precision / recall / F1 of predicted pairs against gold pairs.

`self_join=True` (deduplication within one collection) treats `(i, j)` and
`(j, i)` as one pair and drops `(i, i)`; otherwise pairs are `(row of A, row
of B)` and orientation matters.

* **Return type:**
  [`Scores`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.scores.html.md#equate.evaluate.scores.Scores)

```pycon
>>> s = pairwise_prf([(0, 0), (1, 2)], [(0, 0), (1, 1)])
>>> s.precision, s.recall, s.support
(0.5, 0.5, 2)
```

### equate.evaluate.pr_auc(scores, y_true)

Average precision: the area under the precision-recall step curve.

Records with tied scores enter the ranking together (one threshold step), so the
figure does not depend on the input order of ties. No positives → `nan`.

* **Return type:**
  [`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)

```pycon
>>> round(pr_auc([0.9, 0.8, 0.7, 0.1], [1, 0, 1, 0]), 3)
0.833
```

### equate.evaluate.ranking_metrics(ranked, gold, , ks=(1, 5, 10))

Recall@k, MRR and MAP for ranked candidate lists.

`ranked[q]` is query `q`’s candidates, best first; `gold[q]` is its true match
or a collection of them. Queries with no gold are skipped; a query whose gold never
appears contributes 0.

* **Return type:**
  [`dict`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#dict)

```pycon
>>> m = ranking_metrics({'a': ['x', 'y'], 'b': ['z', 'w']}, {'a': 'y', 'b': 'z'}, ks=(1,))
>>> m['recall_at_1'], m['mrr']
(0.5, 0.75)
```

### equate.evaluate.select_threshold(scores, y_true, , optimize='f1')

The score threshold (`score >= t` predicts a match) that maximises `optimize`.

Pass **validation** scores and labels. `optimize` is `'f1'`, `'precision'` or
`'recall'`; ties go to the higher threshold (fewer predicted matches). Returns the
threshold and the [`Scores`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.html.md#equate.evaluate.Scores) it achieves on the data it was chosen on — which
are therefore optimistic, and are not a test result.

* **Return type:**
  [`tuple`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#tuple)[[`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float), [`Scores`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.scores.html.md#equate.evaluate.scores.Scores)]

```pycon
>>> t, s = select_threshold([0.9, 0.8, 0.4, 0.3], [1, 1, 0, 1])
>>> t, round(s.f1, 3)
(0.3, 0.857)
```

### Modules

| [`benchmark`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.benchmark.html.md#module-equate.evaluate.benchmark)   | Self-benchmarking: a benchmark registry and an honest-by-default harness.      |
|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`labels`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.labels.html.md#module-equate.evaluate.labels)         | Convert between the two granularities: pairs and cluster labels.               |
| [`metrics`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.metrics.html.md#module-equate.evaluate.metrics)       | Pairwise and cluster-level match metrics, dependency-light.                    |
| [`ranking`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.ranking.html.md#module-equate.evaluate.ranking)       | Threshold-free and ranking metrics, and threshold selection as its own step.   |
| [`scores`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.scores.html.md#module-equate.evaluate.scores)         | The one score type every metric returns: precision and recall, never F1 alone. |
| [`split`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.split.html.md#module-equate.evaluate.split)           | Leakage-aware splitting: split over entities, so test entities are unseen.     |


# _autosummary/equate.evaluate.labels.html.md

# equate.evaluate.labels

Convert between the two granularities: pairs and cluster labels.

Pairwise metrics take pair sets; cluster metrics take a label per record. The
conversion is a deliberate act (research doc 14, §2.2): [`pairs_to_labels()`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.labels.html.md#equate.evaluate.labels.pairs_to_labels) takes
the **transitive closure** of a pair set (union-find), which can merge records a matcher
never linked directly, so a user who evaluates a 1:1 matcher with a cluster metric sees
exactly what they are asking for.

### Functions

| [`cross_pairs_to_labels`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.labels.html.md#equate.evaluate.labels.cross_pairs_to_labels)(pairs, \*, n_a, n_b)   | Labels over `A + B` (B's records offset by `n_a`) from two-table `(i, j)` pairs.   |
|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`labels_to_pairs`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.labels.html.md#equate.evaluate.labels.labels_to_pairs)(labels)                      | Every within-cluster pair `(i, j)` with `i < j`.                                   |
| [`pairs_to_labels`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.labels.html.md#equate.evaluate.labels.pairs_to_labels)(pairs, \*, n)                | Cluster label per record `0..n-1` from the transitive closure of `pairs`.          |

### equate.evaluate.labels.cross_pairs_to_labels(pairs, , n_a, n_b)

Labels over `A + B` (B’s records offset by `n_a`) from two-table `(i, j)` pairs.

The bridge from a matching between two collections to the entity view a cluster
metric or an entity split needs.

* **Return type:**
  [`list`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#list)[[`int`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)]

```pycon
>>> cross_pairs_to_labels([(0, 1)], n_a=2, n_b=2)
[0, 1, 2, 0]
```

### equate.evaluate.labels.labels_to_pairs(labels)

Every within-cluster pair `(i, j)` with `i < j`.

* **Return type:**
  [`set`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#set)[[`tuple`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#tuple)[[`int`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int), [`int`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)]]

```pycon
>>> sorted(labels_to_pairs([0, 0, 1, 0]))
[(0, 1), (0, 3), (1, 3)]
```

### equate.evaluate.labels.pairs_to_labels(pairs, , n)

Cluster label per record `0..n-1` from the transitive closure of `pairs`.

Labels are canonical: numbered in order of each cluster’s smallest record, so two
pair sets that induce the same partition give equal label lists. A record no pair
mentions is a singleton.

* **Return type:**
  [`list`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#list)[[`int`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)]

```pycon
>>> pairs_to_labels([(0, 1), (1, 2), (4, 5)], n=6)
[0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 2]
```


# _autosummary/equate.evaluate.metrics.html.md

# equate.evaluate.metrics

Pairwise and cluster-level match metrics, dependency-light.

Two granularities, kept explicit (research doc 14, §2): [`pairwise_prf()`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.metrics.html.md#equate.evaluate.metrics.pairwise_prf) scores pair
sets; [`bcubed()`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.metrics.html.md#equate.evaluate.metrics.bcubed), [`ceaf()`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.metrics.html.md#equate.evaluate.metrics.ceaf) and [`cluster_metrics()`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.metrics.html.md#equate.evaluate.metrics.cluster_metrics) score a label per record.
**B³ is the default cluster metric** — it alone satisfies all of Amigó’s formal
constraints (§2.4) — with CEAF, ARI and V-measure as complements. ARI and V-measure
delegate to `sklearn.metrics` when it is installed and fall back to the numpy
implementations here otherwise; CEAF’s cluster alignment goes through equate’s own
matcher seam rather than a second Hungarian.

### Functions

| [`bcubed`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.metrics.html.md#equate.evaluate.metrics.bcubed)(pred_labels, true_labels)                   | B³ precision / recall / F1 — the default cluster metric.                 |
|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`ceaf`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.metrics.html.md#equate.evaluate.metrics.ceaf)(pred_labels, true_labels, \*[, variant, ...]) | CEAF: score the best one-to-one alignment of predicted to true clusters. |
| [`cluster_metrics`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.metrics.html.md#equate.evaluate.metrics.cluster_metrics)(pred_labels, true_labels, \*)      | B³ (the headline), CEAF-e, ARI, V-measure, homogeneity and completeness. |
| [`pairwise_prf`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.metrics.html.md#equate.evaluate.metrics.pairwise_prf)(pred_pairs, true_pairs, \*[, ...])    | Pairwise precision / recall / F1 of predicted pairs against gold pairs.  |

### equate.evaluate.metrics.bcubed(pred_labels, true_labels)

B³ precision / recall / F1 — the default cluster metric.

Per record: precision is the share of its predicted cluster that truly belongs with
it, recall the share of its true cluster that the prediction kept with it; both are
averaged over records.

* **Return type:**
  [`Scores`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.scores.html.md#equate.evaluate.scores.Scores)

```pycon
>>> s = bcubed([0, 0, 1, 1], [0, 0, 0, 1])
>>> round(s.precision, 3), round(s.recall, 3)
(0.75, 0.667)
```

### equate.evaluate.metrics.ceaf(pred_labels, true_labels, , variant='entity', matcher='optimal')

CEAF: score the best one-to-one alignment of predicted to true clusters.

`variant='entity'` (CEAF-e, φ4) weighs each aligned pair by
`2|K∩R| / (|K|+|R|)` and normalises by the number of clusters;
`variant='mention'` (CEAF-m, φ3) weighs by `|K∩R|` and normalises by the
number of records. The alignment is a maximum-weight assignment, resolved through
equate’s [`matchers`](_autosummary/equate.matching.html.md#equate.matching.matchers) registry (`matcher`), never a
private Hungarian.

* **Return type:**
  [`Scores`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.scores.html.md#equate.evaluate.scores.Scores)

```pycon
>>> round(ceaf([0, 0, 1, 1], [0, 0, 0, 1]).f1, 3)
0.733
```

### equate.evaluate.metrics.cluster_metrics(pred_labels, true_labels, , backend='auto')

B³ (the headline), CEAF-e, ARI, V-measure, homogeneity and completeness.

`backend='auto'` uses `sklearn.metrics` for ARI / V-measure when sklearn is
installed and the numpy implementations otherwise; `'numpy'` forces the latter,
`'sklearn'` requires the former. The two agree; the choice only exists so the
core install needs neither.

* **Return type:**
  [`dict`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#dict)

```pycon
>>> m = cluster_metrics([0, 0, 1, 1], [0, 0, 0, 1], backend='numpy')
>>> sorted(m)
['ari', 'b3_f1', 'b3_precision', 'b3_recall', 'ceaf_e_f1', 'completeness',
 'homogeneity', 'v_measure']
```

### equate.evaluate.metrics.pairwise_prf(pred_pairs, true_pairs, , self_join=False)

Pairwise precision / recall / F1 of predicted pairs against gold pairs.

`self_join=True` (deduplication within one collection) treats `(i, j)` and
`(j, i)` as one pair and drops `(i, i)`; otherwise pairs are `(row of A, row
of B)` and orientation matters.

* **Return type:**
  [`Scores`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.scores.html.md#equate.evaluate.scores.Scores)

```pycon
>>> s = pairwise_prf([(0, 0), (1, 2)], [(0, 0), (1, 1)])
>>> s.precision, s.recall, s.support
(0.5, 0.5, 2)
```


# _autosummary/equate.evaluate.ranking.html.md

# equate.evaluate.ranking

Threshold-free and ranking metrics, and threshold selection as its own step.

[`pr_auc()`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.ranking.html.md#equate.evaluate.ranking.pr_auc) (average precision) summarises a scorer without choosing a threshold and
stays honest under the heavy class imbalance of matching, where ROC-AUC flatters
(research doc 14, §4). [`select_threshold()`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.ranking.html.md#equate.evaluate.ranking.select_threshold) is deliberately separate from scoring:
tuning on the test set should be something a user does on purpose, never by accident
(§3, §7.2).

### Functions

| [`pr_auc`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.ranking.html.md#equate.evaluate.ranking.pr_auc)(scores, y_true)                           | Average precision: the area under the precision-recall step curve.             |
|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`ranking_metrics`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.ranking.html.md#equate.evaluate.ranking.ranking_metrics)(ranked, gold, \*[, ks])          | Recall@k, MRR and MAP for ranked candidate lists.                              |
| [`select_threshold`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.ranking.html.md#equate.evaluate.ranking.select_threshold)(scores, y_true, \*[, optimize]) | The score threshold (`score >= t` predicts a match) that maximises `optimize`. |

### equate.evaluate.ranking.pr_auc(scores, y_true)

Average precision: the area under the precision-recall step curve.

Records with tied scores enter the ranking together (one threshold step), so the
figure does not depend on the input order of ties. No positives → `nan`.

* **Return type:**
  [`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)

```pycon
>>> round(pr_auc([0.9, 0.8, 0.7, 0.1], [1, 0, 1, 0]), 3)
0.833
```

### equate.evaluate.ranking.ranking_metrics(ranked, gold, , ks=(1, 5, 10))

Recall@k, MRR and MAP for ranked candidate lists.

`ranked[q]` is query `q`’s candidates, best first; `gold[q]` is its true match
or a collection of them. Queries with no gold are skipped; a query whose gold never
appears contributes 0.

* **Return type:**
  [`dict`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#dict)

```pycon
>>> m = ranking_metrics({'a': ['x', 'y'], 'b': ['z', 'w']}, {'a': 'y', 'b': 'z'}, ks=(1,))
>>> m['recall_at_1'], m['mrr']
(0.5, 0.75)
```

### equate.evaluate.ranking.select_threshold(scores, y_true, , optimize='f1')

The score threshold (`score >= t` predicts a match) that maximises `optimize`.

Pass **validation** scores and labels. `optimize` is `'f1'`, `'precision'` or
`'recall'`; ties go to the higher threshold (fewer predicted matches). Returns the

# _autosummary/equate.evaluate.scores.html.md

# equate.evaluate.scores

The one score type every metric returns: precision and recall, never F1 alone.

[`Scores`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.scores.html.md#equate.evaluate.scores.Scores) is the SSOT for how a match quality figure is represented (research
doc 14, §2.5): an F1 without the precision/recall it averages hides whether a matcher
is over- or under-linking, so the type carries all three plus the support they were
computed over.

### Classes

| [`Scores`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.scores.html.md#equate.evaluate.scores.Scores)(precision, recall, f1[, support])   | Precision, recall and their harmonic mean, plus what they were computed over.   |
|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------|

### *class* equate.evaluate.scores.Scores(precision, recall, f1, support=None)

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

Precision, recall and their harmonic mean, plus what they were computed over.

```pycon
>>> s = Scores.from_counts(tp=3, n_pred=4, n_true=6)
>>> s.precision, s.recall, round(s.f1, 3)
(0.75, 0.5, 0.6)
>>> s.support
6
```

#### as_dict()

The fields as a plain dict (for tables, JSON, a dataframe row).

* **Return type:**
  [`dict`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#dict)

#### *classmethod* from_counts(, tp, n_pred, n_true)

Build from true-positive, predicted and gold counts.

An empty prediction has precision 1.0 (it asserted nothing false); an empty gold
set has recall 1.0 (there was nothing to find). Both empty is a perfect score.

* **Return type:**
  [`Scores`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.scores.html.md#equate.evaluate.scores.Scores)

#### *classmethod* from_pr(precision, recall, , support=None)

Build from precision and recall; F1 is derived, so it can never disagree.

* **Return type:**
  [`Scores`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.scores.html.md#equate.evaluate.scores.Scores)

#### support *: [int](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int) | [None](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/constants.html#None)* *= None*

the size of the gold side (true pairs, or records for a cluster metric)


# _autosummary/equate.evaluate.split.html.md

# equate.evaluate.split

Leakage-aware splitting: split over entities, so test entities are unseen.

The most common way a matching benchmark lies is a pair-level split: the same real-world
entity shows up in train and test, and the model memorises it (research doc 14, §7.2).
[`entity_split()`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.split.html.md#equate.evaluate.split.entity_split) makes the right split the easy one — it partitions **entity ids**,
so every record of an entity lands in exactly one part — and [`assert_no_leakage()`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.split.html.md#equate.evaluate.split.assert_no_leakage)
is the cheap post-hoc guard for a split made some other way.

### Functions

| [`assert_no_leakage`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.split.html.md#equate.evaluate.split.assert_no_leakage)(entity_ids, \*parts)       | Raise `AssertionError` if any entity has records in more than one of `parts`.   |
|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`entity_split`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.split.html.md#equate.evaluate.split.entity_split)(entity_ids, \*[, ratios, seed]) | Split records into train / val / test by entity, never by record or pair.       |

### Classes

| [`Split`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.split.html.md#equate.evaluate.split.Split)(train, val, test)   | Record indices of each part; the entity ids of a part never occur in another.   |
|----------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------|

### *class* equate.evaluate.split.Split(train, val, test)

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

Record indices of each part; the entity ids of a part never occur in another.

### equate.evaluate.split.assert_no_leakage(entity_ids, \*parts)

Raise `AssertionError` if any entity has records in more than one of `parts`.

* **Return type:**
  [`None`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/constants.html#None)

```pycon
>>> assert_no_leakage([0, 0, 1], [0], [1])
Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...
AssertionError: entity 0 appears in parts 0 and 1 — the split leaks it
```

### equate.evaluate.split.entity_split(entity_ids, , ratios=(0.6, 0.2, 0.2), seed=0)

Split records into train / val / test by entity, never by record or pair.

`entity_ids[i]` is record `i`’s true entity (e.g. from
[`cross_pairs_to_labels()`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.html.md#equate.evaluate.cross_pairs_to_labels) over a two-table gold matching).
Entities, not records, are shuffled (`seed`) and cut by `ratios`, so the parts
are disjoint in entities and roughly — not exactly — proportional in records.

* **Return type:**
  [`Split`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.split.html.md#equate.evaluate.split.Split)

```pycon
>>> s = entity_split([0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 6], seed=1)
>>> assert_no_leakage([0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 6], s.train, s.test)
>>> sorted(s.train + s.val + s.test) == list(range(10))
True
```


# _autosummary/equate.facade.html.md

# equate.facade

The equate facade: the one-line `match(A, B)` entry point.

Wires the pipeline — featurize → compare (over the blocker’s candidates) → match — with
sensible defaults, and returns a structured [`equate.base.Matching`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.Matching). Every stage is
swappable by one keyword (decision register D4): `featurize=`, `compare=`, `block=`,
`how=`. This is the canonical case (doc 10 §1): two collections -> optimally-matched
(and scored) pairs, zero config.

### Functions

| [`match`](_autosummary/equate.facade.html.md#equate.facade.match)(A[, B, featurize, compare, block, ...])   | Match two collections into a [`Matching`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.Matching) of scored `(i, j)` pairs.                                  |
|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`dedupe`](_autosummary/equate.facade.html.md#equate.facade.dedupe)(A, \*[, compare, block, threshold, ...]) | Deduplicate a single collection into entity groups.                                                                                                                    |
| [`resolve`](_autosummary/equate.facade.html.md#equate.facade.resolve)(\*collections, \*\*kwargs)              | Resolve entities across multiple collections: pool them (in order) and [`dedupe()`](_autosummary/equate.facade.html.md#equate.facade.dedupe) -> a Partition over the pooled items. |

### equate.facade.dedupe(A, , compare='ratio', block=None, threshold=0.7, cluster='connected_components', sense=None)

Deduplicate a single collection into entity groups.

Self-compares `A`’s candidate pairs, keeps those passing `threshold`, and clusters
them -> a [`Partition`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.Partition) over `A` (iterate it for the duplicate
`(i, j)` pairs; `.groups()` for the clusters). `block` (a blocker) restricts the
candidate pairs (self-join); the default compares all `i < j` pairs. `cluster` is
`'connected_components'` (transitive closure) or `'correlation'`. `sense` defaults
to the comparator’s declared polarity — a *distance* comparator (e.g.
`levenshtein_distance`) uses `'minimize'` so *lower* scores link, a similarity uses
`'maximize'`.

```pycon
>>> from equate import dedupe
>>> dedupe(['Jon Smith', 'Jon Smyth', 'Kate Doe'], threshold=0.8).groups()
{0: [0, 1], 1: [2]}
```

### equate.facade.match(A, B=None, , featurize=None, compare=None, block=None, how='assign', threshold=None, cluster='connected_components', sense='maximize')

Match two collections into a [`Matching`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.Matching) of scored `(i, j)` pairs.

Pipeline (each stage swappable by one keyword):

- **featurize / compare** — with `compare=None` (default), the *vector route*:
  featurize both sides with `featurize` (TF-IDF by default) and score by cosine.
  With a `compare` comparator (a registered name or a callable), the \*direct
  pairwise route\* on the raw items.
- **block** — `None` (default) scores all pairs (dense); a blocker (name/callable)
  scores only the candidate pairs into a sparse matrix, and the matcher stays sparse-aware.
- **how** — the matcher objective: `'assign'` (optimal 1:1, the default),
  `'greedy'`, `'stable'`, or `'soft'` (an optimal-transport plan; `.plan` is set).

Returns a `Matching`: iterate it for `(i, j)` pairs, `dict(...)` it for a mapping,
`.labeled_pairs()` for `(A[i], B[j])`; `.scores` holds each matched pair’s score.

```pycon
>>> keys = ['apple pie', 'banana split', 'cherry tart']
>>> values = ['cherry tarte', 'aple pie', 'banana split']
>>> m = match(keys, values, compare='ratio')
>>> dict(m.labeled_pairs())
{'apple pie': 'aple pie', 'banana split': 'banana split', 'cherry tart': 'cherry tarte'}
```

### equate.facade.resolve(\*collections, \*\*kwargs)

Resolve entities across multiple collections: pool them (in order) and
[`dedupe()`](_autosummary/equate.facade.html.md#equate.facade.dedupe) -> a Partition over the pooled items. Generalizes cross-collection
matching to n-way linkage. Accepts the same keywords as [`dedupe()`](_autosummary/equate.facade.html.md#equate.facade.dedupe).


# _autosummary/equate.featurize.html.md

# equate.featurize

The featurize stage (①): map objects to comparable representations.

A *featurizer* is a batch callable `Iterable[object] -> representations`. The default
is a pure numpy/scipy char-n-gram TF-IDF ([`equate.featurize.tfidf`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.tfidf.html.md#module-equate.featurize.tfidf)) — no heavy
dependencies; dense embedders (SBERT, OpenAI, …) are optional extras
([`equate.featurize.text`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.text.html.md#module-equate.featurize.text)). Select a featurizer by name via the [`featurizers`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.html.md#equate.featurize.featurizers)
registry, or pass a callable. Corpus-dependent featurizers (TF-IDF) are built by
fitting on a corpus, which [`resolve_featurizer()`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.html.md#equate.featurize.resolve_featurizer) handles.

### Module Attributes

| [`featurizers`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.html.md#equate.featurize.featurizers)   | the featurize-stage strategy registry (name -> lazy factory)   |
|----------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------|

### Functions

| [`identity`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.html.md#equate.featurize.identity)(objects)                                 | The identity featurizer: use the objects themselves as their representation.                                                                                                                      |
|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`resolve_featurizer`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.html.md#equate.featurize.resolve_featurizer)([spec, corpus])                | Resolve `spec` to a ready-to-use batch featurizer.                                                                                                                                                |
| [`mk_tfidf`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.html.md#equate.featurize.mk_tfidf)(\*learn_texts[, ngram_range, lowercase]) | Fit a char-n-gram TF-IDF on the given collection(s) and return the fitted, callable batch featurizer — the pure numpy/scipy replacement for the legacy grub-backed `equate.util.mk_text_to_vect`. |
| [`char_ngrams`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.html.md#equate.featurize.char_ngrams)(text[, ngram_range, lowercase])       | Character n-grams of `text` over the inclusive `ngram_range`.                                                                                                                                     |

### Classes

| [`TfidfFeaturizer`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.html.md#equate.featurize.TfidfFeaturizer)(\*[, ngram_range, lowercase])   | Fittable char-n-gram TF-IDF featurizer producing L2-normalized sparse vectors.                                                                                                                                                                  |
|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`FeaturizerMeta`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.html.md#equate.featurize.FeaturizerMeta)([output_kinds, normalize, ...])  | Declared properties of a featurizer (decision register D9), so the framework can pick a legal index/metric, auto-apply a required query/passage prefix, refuse a non-commercial model in a commercial context, and offer Matryoshka truncation. |

### *class* equate.featurize.FeaturizerMeta(output_kinds=('vector',), normalize=False, dim=None, license=None, max_seq_len=None, query_prefix=None, passage_prefix=None, truncatable_to=())

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

Declared properties of a featurizer (decision register D9), so the framework
can pick a legal index/metric, auto-apply a required query/passage prefix, refuse a
non-commercial model in a commercial context, and offer Matryoshka truncation.

- `output_kinds`: what the representation is — `'vector'` / `'set'` /
  `'bitstring'` / `'scalar'` / `'structured'` (a multi-functional embedder may
  emit several, e.g. dense + sparse);
- `normalize`: whether output vectors are already L2-normalized;
- `dim` / `max_seq_len`: dimensionality and max input length, when fixed;
- `license`: SPDX/label, so a commercial context can refuse non-commercial models;
- `query_prefix` / `passage_prefix`: instruction prefixes some embedders require
  (e.g. E5’s `"query: "` / `"passage: "`) — a silent-omission footgun;
- `truncatable_to`: Matryoshka dims the embedding can be safely truncated to.

### *class* equate.featurize.TfidfFeaturizer(, ngram_range=(2, 4), lowercase=True)

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

Fittable char-n-gram TF-IDF featurizer producing L2-normalized sparse vectors.

Fit on a corpus to learn the vocabulary and inverse document frequencies, then
transform texts to vectors. A fitted instance is itself a batch featurizer, so
`vecs = featurizer(texts)` works.

#### meta *= FeaturizerMeta(output_kinds=('vector',), normalize=True, dim=None, license='core', max_seq_len=None, query_prefix=None, passage_prefix=None, truncatable_to=())*

declared metadata (see equate.base.FeaturizerMeta)

### equate.featurize.char_ngrams(text, ngram_range=(2, 4), , lowercase=True)

Character n-grams of `text` over the inclusive `ngram_range`.

The whole string is padded with one leading and one trailing space (so prefixes and
suffixes are captured), and n-grams slide over the entire padded string — they \*may
therefore span the spaces between words\*. This is deliberate (it helps fuzzy
name/SKU matching) and differs from scikit-learn’s per-word `char_wb` analyzer. A
text too short for any `n` in the range falls back to the padded string itself, so
tiny or empty inputs still yield a (single) feature rather than an all-zero vector.

```pycon
>>> char_ngrams('cat', (2, 3))
[' c', 'ca', 'at', 't ', ' ca', 'cat', 'at ']
>>> char_ngrams('', (3, 4))          # too short for any n: falls back to the padding
['  ']
```

### equate.featurize.featurizers *= <equate.registry.Registry object>*

the featurize-stage strategy registry (name -> lazy factory)

### equate.featurize.identity(objects)

The identity featurizer: use the objects themselves as their representation.

This is the degenerate case that recovers exact matching (φ = id).

### equate.featurize.mk_tfidf(\*learn_texts, ngram_range=(2, 4), lowercase=True)

Fit a char-n-gram TF-IDF on the given collection(s) and return the fitted,
callable batch featurizer — the pure numpy/scipy replacement for the legacy
grub-backed `equate.util.mk_text_to_vect`.

### equate.featurize.resolve_featurizer(spec=None, , corpus=None, \*\*config)

Resolve `spec` to a ready-to-use batch featurizer.

- `None` -> the default `'tfidf'`;
- a registered name (`str`) -> built via its factory (`**config` is forwarded, so
  an unknown option raises rather than being silently ignored);
- a callable -> returned as-is (assumed already a batch featurizer).

A *fittable* featurizer (one exposing `fit`, e.g. TF-IDF) is fit on `corpus`
here — and a corpus is then required: resolving a fittable featurizer without one
raises immediately (a clear error at the call site) instead of returning a
half-built object that only fails later inside `transform`.

### Modules

| [`text`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.text.html.md#module-equate.featurize.text)   | Dense text-embedding featurizers, behind optional extras.                                                                 |
|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`tfidf`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.tfidf.html.md#module-equate.featurize.tfidf) | Pure-numpy/scipy character-n-gram TF-IDF — equate's zero-heavy-dependency default text featurizer (decision register D9). |


# _autosummary/equate.featurize.text.html.md

# equate.featurize.text

Dense text-embedding featurizers, behind optional extras.

Each is a *lazily-built* strategy: the heavy library is imported only when the
strategy is actually constructed, via `equate._dependencies.require()`, so a
missing extra raises a friendly `MissingDependencyError` instead of breaking
`import equate`. A representative set is provided here; more embedders (bge-m3, e5,
nomic, cohere, voyage, and image/audio modalities) are added the same way as their
stages land — see the `equate-dev-add-strategy` skill.

|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------|

OpenAI embeddings — requires `equate[api]` and an `OPENAI_API_KEY`.

Pure-numpy/scipy character-n-gram TF-IDF — equate’s zero-heavy-dependency default
text featurizer (decision register D9). No scikit-learn or grub required.

matching; the output vectors are L2-normalized, so cosine similarity is a dot product.

# _autosummary/equate.html.md

# equate

Tools for matching things: featurize, compare, and match collections of objects.

Matching is fuzzy correspondence, not exact equality (`==` is the degenerate case).
The public surface is being redesigned around the `featurize -> compare -> match`
decomposition; see `docs/research/` and the `equate-dev-architecture` skill. The
foundation contracts live in [`equate.base`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#module-equate.base).

### Modules

| [`base`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#module-equate.base)               | Foundational contracts and data structures for equate.                              |
|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`block`](_autosummary/equate.block.html.md#module-equate.block)             | The block stage (② scalability): candidate generation.                              |
| [`cluster`](_autosummary/equate.cluster.html.md#module-equate.cluster)         | The resolve/cluster stage (③ grouping): turn pairwise matches into entity groups.   |
| [`compare`](_autosummary/equate.compare.html.md#module-equate.compare)         | The compare stage (②): score how alike two (featurized) items are.                  |
| [`completion`](_autosummary/equate.completion.html.md#module-equate.completion)   | Tools to complete missing data from other sources of the same data.                 |
| [`evaluate`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.html.md#module-equate.evaluate)       | Evaluate matchers honestly: metrics, leakage-aware splits, and a benchmark harness. |
| [`facade`](_autosummary/equate.facade.html.md#module-equate.facade)           | The equate facade: the one-line `match(A, B)` entry point.                          |
| [`featurize`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.html.md#module-equate.featurize)     | The featurize stage (①): map objects to comparable representations.                 |
| [`interactive`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.html.md#module-equate.interactive) | The interactive stage: human-in-the-loop review and re-optimization.                |
| [`matching`](_autosummary/equate.matching.html.md#module-equate.matching)       | The match stage (③): turn a score matrix into a correspondence.                     |
| [`registry`](_autosummary/equate.registry.html.md#module-equate.registry)       | A tiny name-keyed strategy registry with lazy factories (open-closed dispatch).     |
| [`util`](_autosummary/equate.util.html.md#module-equate.util)               | Utils for equate.                                                                   |


# _autosummary/equate.interactive.candidate_store.html.md

# equate.interactive.candidate_store

The CandidateStore: per left-item top-k candidates with scores — the SSOT for review
and interactive re-optimization.

Retaining the top-k candidates (not just the single best) is what lets a user edit a match
and have the system re-solve from the remembered alternatives (doc 08-interactive). It is a
plain dataclass so it serializes (e.g. persist with `dol.cache_this` to resume a session).

### Classes

| [`CandidateStore`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.candidate_store.html.md#equate.interactive.candidate_store.CandidateStore)(candidates[, sense, ...])   | Per left index `i`, its top-k `(right_index, score)` candidates, best-first.   |
|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|

### *class* equate.interactive.candidate_store.CandidateStore(candidates, sense='maximize', row_labels=None, col_labels=None)

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

Per left index `i`, its top-k `(right_index, score)` candidates, best-first.

Iterating yields the top-1 `(i, j)` pairs, so `dict(store)` gives the greedy 1:n
match. `row_labels` / `col_labels` name the two collections.

#### *classmethod* from_scores(scores, , k=5, sense='maximize', row_labels=None, col_labels=None)

Build a store of each row’s top-`k` candidates from a (dense or sparse) score
matrix.

A **sparse** matrix considers only its stored (candidate) cells — which is exactly
the blocking semantics (an absent cell is not a candidate), so for a blocked matrix
this intentionally differs from the dense all-cells behavior regardless of `sense`.

#### margin(i)

Confidence gap between item `i`’s top-1 and top-2 candidate scores.

A *small* margin means the top choice is uncertain (two close candidates) — the
signal for review triage and active-learning query selection. An item with 0 or 1
candidates is unambiguous (no rival to be confused with), so its margin is `+inf`
— it sorts LAST in a most-uncertain-first queue, never spuriously to the front.

#### top(i, n=1)

The top-`n` `(right_index, score)` candidates for left item `i`.


# _autosummary/equate.interactive.constraints.html.md

# equate.interactive.constraints

Interactive constraints and re-optimization: every user edit is a constraint, not a
recompute.

A *confirm* forces an edge into the assignment; a *reject* forbids one. [`reoptimize()`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.constraints.html.md#equate.interactive.constraints.reoptimize)
re-solves the optimal assignment honoring the accumulated constraints — the primitive
behind “edit a match and the system updates the rest from the remembered alternatives”
(doc 08-interactive). The constraint set is append-only so a session’s edit history is a
replayable log.

### Functions

| [`reoptimize`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.constraints.html.md#equate.interactive.constraints.reoptimize)(scores[, constraints, sense])   | Re-solve the optimal 1:1 assignment honoring `constraints` (confirmed/rejected).   |
|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|

### Classes

| [`ConstraintSet`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.constraints.html.md#equate.interactive.constraints.ConstraintSet)([forced, forbidden])   | Append-only record of user edits: `forced` (confirmed) and `forbidden` (rejected) `(i, j)` edges.   |
|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|

### *class* equate.interactive.constraints.ConstraintSet(forced=<factory>, forbidden=<factory>)

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

Append-only record of user edits: `forced` (confirmed) and `forbidden`
(rejected) `(i, j)` edges.

#### confirm(i, j)

Force edge `(i, j)` into the assignment (a user-confirmed match).

#### reject(i, j)

Forbid edge `(i, j)` from the assignment (a user-rejected match).

### equate.interactive.constraints.reoptimize(scores, constraints=None, , sense='maximize')

Re-solve the optimal 1:1 assignment honoring `constraints` (confirmed/rejected).

Returns the matched `(i, j)` pairs. Raises `ValueError` if the constraints are
infeasible (no valid assignment). This is O(one LAP): the whole point is that an edit
is a cheap constrained re-solve, not a from-scratch recompute.


# _autosummary/equate.interactive.html.md

# equate.interactive

The interactive stage: human-in-the-loop review and re-optimization.

The payoff of retaining **top-k candidates with scores** (doc 08-interactive): a user can
edit a match and the system re-solves the rest from the remembered alternatives. The pieces:

- [`CandidateStore`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.html.md#equate.interactive.CandidateStore) — the per-item top-k SSOT (built from a score matrix; serializable);
- [`k_best_assignments()`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.html.md#equate.interactive.k_best_assignments) — Murty’s k-best global matchings, in order (in-house, pure scipy);
- [`ConstraintSet`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.html.md#equate.interactive.ConstraintSet) + [`reoptimize()`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.html.md#equate.interactive.reoptimize) — every edit is a force/forbid constraint,
  re-solved with one constrained LAP, not a from-scratch recompute;
- [`review_queue()`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.html.md#equate.interactive.review_queue) / [`uncertainty_sampling()`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.html.md#equate.interactive.uncertainty_sampling) — rank items by confidence margin for
  human review and active-learning query selection.

Structured explanations use [`equate.base.Explanation`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.Explanation). Heavier active-learning
backends (modAL / scikit-activeml) are optional (`equate[active]`); the margin-based
query strategy here needs no extra.

### Functions

| [`k_best_assignments`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.html.md#equate.interactive.k_best_assignments)(cost, k)                    | The `k` lowest-cost assignments of `cost`, in increasing-cost order (Murty).                          |
|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`solve_constrained`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.html.md#equate.interactive.solve_constrained)(cost[, forced, forbidden])   | Minimum-cost assignment of `cost` with edge constraints.                                              |
| [`reoptimize`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.html.md#equate.interactive.reoptimize)(scores[, constraints, sense])       | Re-solve the optimal 1:1 assignment honoring `constraints` (confirmed/rejected).                      |
| [`review_queue`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.html.md#equate.interactive.review_queue)(candidate_store, \*[, ...])       | Order the left items of a [`CandidateStore`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.html.md#equate.interactive.CandidateStore) for review. |
| [`uncertainty_sampling`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.html.md#equate.interactive.uncertainty_sampling)(candidate_store, \*[, n]) | Active-learning query: the `n` most uncertain items to label next.                                    |

### Classes

| [`CandidateStore`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.html.md#equate.interactive.CandidateStore)(candidates[, sense, ...])   | Per left index `i`, its top-k `(right_index, score)` candidates, best-first.                      |
|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`ConstraintSet`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.html.md#equate.interactive.ConstraintSet)([forced, forbidden])         | Append-only record of user edits: `forced` (confirmed) and `forbidden` (rejected) `(i, j)` edges. |

### *class* equate.interactive.CandidateStore(candidates, sense='maximize', row_labels=None, col_labels=None)

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

Per left index `i`, its top-k `(right_index, score)` candidates, best-first.

Iterating yields the top-1 `(i, j)` pairs, so `dict(store)` gives the greedy 1:n
match. `row_labels` / `col_labels` name the two collections.

#### *classmethod* from_scores(scores, , k=5, sense='maximize', row_labels=None, col_labels=None)

Build a store of each row’s top-`k` candidates from a (dense or sparse) score
matrix.

A **sparse** matrix considers only its stored (candidate) cells — which is exactly
the blocking semantics (an absent cell is not a candidate), so for a blocked matrix
this intentionally differs from the dense all-cells behavior regardless of `sense`.

#### margin(i)

Confidence gap between item `i`’s top-1 and top-2 candidate scores.

A *small* margin means the top choice is uncertain (two close candidates) — the
signal for review triage and active-learning query selection. An item with 0 or 1
candidates is unambiguous (no rival to be confused with), so its margin is `+inf`
— it sorts LAST in a most-uncertain-first queue, never spuriously to the front.

#### top(i, n=1)

The top-`n` `(right_index, score)` candidates for left item `i`.

### *class* equate.interactive.ConstraintSet(forced=<factory>, forbidden=<factory>)

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

Append-only record of user edits: `forced` (confirmed) and `forbidden`
(rejected) `(i, j)` edges.

#### confirm(i, j)

Force edge `(i, j)` into the assignment (a user-confirmed match).

#### reject(i, j)

Forbid edge `(i, j)` from the assignment (a user-rejected match).

### equate.interactive.k_best_assignments(cost, k)

The `k` lowest-cost assignments of `cost`, in increasing-cost order (Murty).

Returns a list of `(assignment: {i: j}, total_cost)` — fewer than `k` if there are
not that many feasible assignments.

```pycon
>>> [c for _, c in k_best_assignments([[1, 2], [2, 1]], 2)]
[2.0, 4.0]
```

### equate.interactive.reoptimize(scores, constraints=None, , sense='maximize')

Re-solve the optimal 1:1 assignment honoring `constraints` (confirmed/rejected).

Returns the matched `(i, j)` pairs. Raises `ValueError` if the constraints are
infeasible (no valid assignment). This is O(one LAP): the whole point is that an edit
is a cheap constrained re-solve, not a from-scratch recompute.

### equate.interactive.review_queue(candidate_store, , most_uncertain_first=True)

Order the left items of a [`CandidateStore`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.html.md#equate.interactive.CandidateStore) for review.

By default the most-uncertain items (smallest top-1/top-2 margin) come first — the
decisions a human should look at soonest.

### equate.interactive.solve_constrained(cost, forced=(), forbidden=())

Minimum-cost assignment of `cost` with edge constraints.

`forced` = `(i, j)` edges that MUST be in the assignment; `forbidden` = `(i, j)`
edges that must NOT. Returns `(assignment: {i: j}, total_cost)` or `None` if the
constraints admit no valid assignment.

### equate.interactive.uncertainty_sampling(candidate_store, , n=10)

Active-learning query: the `n` most uncertain items to label next.

Uncertainty sampling — label the items whose top choice is least certain (smallest
margin), since those labels are the most informative for training a matcher.

# _autosummary/equate.interactive.kbest.html.md

# equate.interactive.kbest

k-best assignments via Murty’s algorithm (in-house; pure numpy/scipy).

Enumerating the k lowest-cost assignments *in order* is the substrate for interactive
re-optimization: retain the top-k global matchings so that when a user confirms or rejects
an edge, the next-best consistent assignment is already known (decision register D10 /
doc 08-interactive). No well-maintained pure-Python Murty exists on PyPI, so equate ships
one. `solve_constrained` (a LAP with forced / forbidden edges) is also the primitive the
interactive re-optimization uses directly.

### Functions

| [`solve_constrained`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.kbest.html.md#equate.interactive.kbest.solve_constrained)(cost[, forced, forbidden])   | Minimum-cost assignment of `cost` with edge constraints.                     |
|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`k_best_assignments`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.kbest.html.md#equate.interactive.kbest.k_best_assignments)(cost, k)                    | The `k` lowest-cost assignments of `cost`, in increasing-cost order (Murty). |

### equate.interactive.kbest.k_best_assignments(cost, k)

The `k` lowest-cost assignments of `cost`, in increasing-cost order (Murty).

Returns a list of `(assignment: {i: j}, total_cost)` — fewer than `k` if there are
not that many feasible assignments.

```pycon
>>> [c for _, c in k_best_assignments([[1, 2], [2, 1]], 2)]
[2.0, 4.0]
```

### equate.interactive.kbest.solve_constrained(cost, forced=(), forbidden=())

Minimum-cost assignment of `cost` with edge constraints.

`forced` = `(i, j)` edges that MUST be in the assignment; `forbidden` = `(i, j)`
edges that must NOT. Returns `(assignment: {i: j}, total_cost)` or `None` if the
constraints admit no valid assignment.

# equate.interactive.review

Human review triage and active-learning query selection.

Both rank items by *uncertainty* — the confidence margin between an item’s top-1 and top-2
candidates (small margin = an ambiguous, review-worthy decision). [`review_queue()`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.review.html.md#equate.interactive.review.review_queue)
orders items for a verification UI; [`uncertainty_sampling()`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.review.html.md#equate.interactive.review.uncertainty_sampling) picks the most-informative
items for an oracle to label (active learning). An `Oracle` is any callable
`(i, j) -> bool` (a human, an LLM, or a crowd) — kept as a plain protocol, not a class.

# _autosummary/equate.matching.assign.html.md

# equate.matching.assign

Assignment matchers (stage ③): turn a score matrix into matched `(i, j)` pairs.

Expose the *objective* (optimal / greedy / stable), not the algorithm. The optimal
matcher is **sparse-aware**: a blocked (sparse) score matrix routes to the sparse LAP
solver instead of densifying. All route similarity→cost through the `to_cost` SSOT
(decision register D2), so a `sense` of `'maximize'` (similarity) or `'minimize'`
(distance) is honored consistently.

### Functions

| [`optimal_matching`](_autosummary/equate.matching.assign.html.md#equate.matching.assign.optimal_matching)(scores, \*[, sense])   | Globally optimal 1:1 assignment (the linear assignment problem).              |
|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`greedy_matching`](_autosummary/equate.matching.assign.html.md#equate.matching.assign.greedy_matching)(scores, \*[, sense])    | Greedy 1:1: repeatedly take the best still-available `(i, j)`, removing both. |
| [`stable_matching`](_autosummary/equate.matching.assign.html.md#equate.matching.assign.stable_matching)(scores, \*[, sense])    | Gale-Shapley stable matching (optimizes stability, not total score).          |

### equate.matching.assign.greedy_matching(scores, , sense=None)

Greedy 1:1: repeatedly take the best still-available `(i, j)`, removing both.

Order-dependent and not globally optimal, but fast. Iterates
[`stored_entries()`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.ScoreMatrix.stored_entries), so for a sparse (blocked) matrix only
the stored candidate cells are considered — an absent cell is never a match.

### equate.matching.assign.optimal_matching(scores, , sense=None)

Globally optimal 1:1 assignment (the linear assignment problem).

Accepts a [`ScoreMatrix`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.ScoreMatrix) (native) or a raw dense/sparse array with
`sense=` (back-compat). Solves `linear_sum_assignment` on
[`dense_cost()`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.ScoreMatrix.dense_cost) — so a **sparse (blocked)** matrix has its
absent cells worst-cased (never preferred over a real pair) and any assignment landing
on a non-candidate cell is dropped via [`candidate_mask()`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.ScoreMatrix.candidate_mask):
a row with no candidate is left unmatched (a *partial* matching), an all-absent matrix
yields no matches. Densifying the cost is a correctness stopgap; a non-densifying
sparse LAP is a future optimization (scipy’s sparse solver silently drops
explicitly-stored zero-score candidates, so it is not used here).

### equate.matching.assign.stable_matching(scores, , sense=None)

Gale-Shapley stable matching (optimizes stability, not total score).

See [`equate.util.stable_marriage_matching()`](_autosummary/equate.util.html.md#equate.util.stable_marriage_matching). Ranks preferences by
[`dense_cost()`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.ScoreMatrix.dense_cost) (absent cells worst-cased), so a sparse
(blocked) cell never out-ranks a real candidate; hole-assignments are then dropped via
[`candidate_mask()`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.ScoreMatrix.candidate_mask).


# _autosummary/equate.matching.html.md

# equate.matching

The match stage (③): turn a score matrix into a correspondence.

A *Matcher* is a strategy over a score structure — the choice is the **objective**, not
the algorithm (decision register D4). Select by name via the [`matchers`](_autosummary/equate.matching.html.md#equate.matching.matchers) registry or
pass a callable `(scores, *, sense) -> pairs`. The optimal matcher is sparse-aware
(routes a blocked matrix to the sparse LAP); soft matching (optimal transport) lives in a
parallel [`soft_match()`](_autosummary/equate.matching.html.md#equate.matching.soft_match) / [`harden()`](_autosummary/equate.matching.html.md#equate.matching.harden) seam.

### Module Attributes

| [`matchers`](_autosummary/equate.matching.html.md#equate.matching.matchers)   | the match-stage strategy registry (name -> lazy factory)   |
|-------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------|

### Functions

| [`resolve_matcher`](_autosummary/equate.matching.html.md#equate.matching.resolve_matcher)([spec])                    | Resolve `spec` to a runner `(scores_or_scorematrix, *, sense=None) -> pairs`.   |
|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`optimal_matching`](_autosummary/equate.matching.html.md#equate.matching.optimal_matching)(scores, \*[, sense])      | Globally optimal 1:1 assignment (the linear assignment problem).                |
| [`greedy_matching`](_autosummary/equate.matching.html.md#equate.matching.greedy_matching)(scores, \*[, sense])       | Greedy 1:1: repeatedly take the best still-available `(i, j)`, removing both.   |
| [`stable_matching`](_autosummary/equate.matching.html.md#equate.matching.stable_matching)(scores, \*[, sense])       | Gale-Shapley stable matching (optimizes stability, not total score).            |
| [`soft_match`](_autosummary/equate.matching.html.md#equate.matching.soft_match)(scores, \*[, sense, reg, a, b]) | Entropic optimal-transport (Sinkhorn) plan over the cost derived from `scores`. |
| [`harden`](_autosummary/equate.matching.html.md#equate.matching.harden)(plan)                               | Recover a hard 1:1 assignment from a transport `plan` (LAP maximizing mass).    |

### equate.matching.greedy_matching(scores, , sense=None)

Greedy 1:1: repeatedly take the best still-available `(i, j)`, removing both.

Order-dependent and not globally optimal, but fast. Iterates
[`stored_entries()`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.ScoreMatrix.stored_entries), so for a sparse (blocked) matrix only
the stored candidate cells are considered — an absent cell is never a match.

### equate.matching.harden(plan)

Recover a hard 1:1 assignment from a transport `plan` (LAP maximizing mass).

### equate.matching.matchers *= <equate.registry.Registry object>*

the match-stage strategy registry (name -> lazy factory)

### equate.matching.optimal_matching(scores, , sense=None)

Globally optimal 1:1 assignment (the linear assignment problem).

Accepts a [`ScoreMatrix`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.ScoreMatrix) (native) or a raw dense/sparse array with
`sense=` (back-compat). Solves `linear_sum_assignment` on
[`dense_cost()`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.ScoreMatrix.dense_cost) — so a **sparse (blocked)** matrix has its
absent cells worst-cased (never preferred over a real pair) and any assignment landing
on a non-candidate cell is dropped via [`candidate_mask()`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.ScoreMatrix.candidate_mask):
a row with no candidate is left unmatched (a *partial* matching), an all-absent matrix
yields no matches. Densifying the cost is a correctness stopgap; a non-densifying
sparse LAP is a future optimization (scipy’s sparse solver silently drops
explicitly-stored zero-score candidates, so it is not used here).

### equate.matching.resolve_matcher(spec='optimal', \*\*config)

Resolve `spec` to a runner `(scores_or_scorematrix, *, sense=None) -> pairs`.

A registered name (or a facade `how=` alias like `'assign' -> 'optimal'`) is built
via the registry; a callable is used as-is. The returned runner coerces its argument to
a [`ScoreMatrix`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.ScoreMatrix) and then either hands that matrix to a **native**
matcher (so it worst-cases holes through the sanctioned views) or hands a **legacy**
raw-array matcher a hole-worst-cased dense array — so the sparse hole-worst-casing holds
no matter which contract the matcher follows (D11).

Note this returns a *runner*, not `spec` itself: unlike the pre-D11 version it is no
longer an identity passthrough for a callable (`resolve_matcher(f) is f` was true, and
is not any more). The runner carries the wrapped matcher’s `__name__`/`__doc__`, and
the original is recoverable via `__wrapped__`.

### equate.matching.soft_match(scores, , sense=None, reg=0.1, a=None, b=None)

Entropic optimal-transport (Sinkhorn) plan over the cost derived from `scores`.

Accepts a [`ScoreMatrix`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.ScoreMatrix) (native) or a raw array with `sense=`.
Returns a dense transport-plan matrix whose rows/cols sum to the marginals `a`/`b`
(uniform by default). Requires `equate[ot]` (POT). `reg` (entropic regularization)
must be > 0 (`reg=0` divides by zero inside Sinkhorn).

### equate.matching.stable_matching(scores, , sense=None)

Gale-Shapley stable matching (optimizes stability, not total score).

See [`equate.util.stable_marriage_matching()`](_autosummary/equate.util.html.md#equate.util.stable_marriage_matching). Ranks preferences by
[`dense_cost()`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.ScoreMatrix.dense_cost) (absent cells worst-cased), so a sparse
(blocked) cell never out-ranks a real candidate; hole-assignments are then dropped via
[`candidate_mask()`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.ScoreMatrix.candidate_mask).

### Modules

| [`assign`](_autosummary/equate.matching.assign.html.md#module-equate.matching.assign)   | Assignment matchers (stage ③): turn a score matrix into matched `(i, j)` pairs.                                                                                                                                                                  |
|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`soft`](_autosummary/equate.matching.soft.html.md#module-equate.matching.soft)       | Soft / optimal-transport matching (stage ③): a fractional transport plan rather than a hard assignment — the home for graded, partial, unequal-mass and cross-modal matching (and, later, soft-DTW / Gromov-Wasserstein — decision register D8). |

# _autosummary/equate.registry.html.md

# equate.registry

A tiny name-keyed strategy registry with lazy factories (open-closed dispatch).

Each pipeline stage (featurize, compare, block, match, cluster) owns a `Registry`
mapping a string `name` to a lazy factory that builds the strategy on demand, so a
heavy optional import fires only when that strategy is actually used. Users select a
strategy by name (`featurize='tfidf'`) or pass a callable directly — [`Registry.resolve()`](_autosummary/equate.registry.html.md#equate.registry.Registry.resolve)
accepts both, and users can register their own strategies without subclassing.

### Classes

| [`Registry`](_autosummary/equate.registry.html.md#equate.registry.Registry)(kind)   | A `name -> lazy factory` registry for one pipeline stage's strategies.   |
|-------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------|

### *class* equate.registry.Registry(kind)

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

A `name -> lazy factory` registry for one pipeline stage’s strategies.

```pycon
>>> reg = Registry('demo')
>>> @reg.register('double')
... def _double_factory():
...     return lambda x: x * 2
>>> reg.names()
['double']
>>> reg.create('double')(21)          # look up + build + call
42
>>> reg.resolve(str.upper)('hi')       # a callable passes through unchanged
'HI'
>>> 'double' in reg
True
```

#### create(name, \*args, \*\*kwargs)

Build the strategy registered under `name` (calls its lazy factory).

#### factory(name)

Return the (uncalled) factory registered under `name`.

* **Return type:**
  [`Callable`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.Callable)

#### meta(name)

Return the declared metadata for `name` (`None` if none was declared).

Raises `KeyError` for an unknown name, consistent with [`factory()`](_autosummary/equate.registry.html.md#equate.registry.Registry.factory) — so
an unknown name is never silently conflated with a known name that has no meta.

* **Return type:**
  [`Any`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Any)

#### names()

Sorted list of registered strategy names.

* **Return type:**
  [`list`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#list)

#### register(name, factory=None, , meta=None)

Register `factory` under `name`. Usable as a decorator or directly.

The factory is called lazily (by [`create()`](_autosummary/equate.registry.html.md#equate.registry.Registry.create)/[`resolve()`](_autosummary/equate.registry.html.md#equate.registry.Registry.resolve)), so any heavy
import inside it fires only on use. `meta` is optional declared metadata
(e.g. a `FeaturizerMeta`/`ComparatorMeta`).

#### resolve(spec, \*args, \*\*kwargs)

Resolve `spec` to a strategy.

A callable `spec` passes through unchanged; a `str` is looked up and its
factory is called with `(*args, **kwargs)`.
